body:
The Mauryan period and the growth of monumental art

The Mauryan Empire was established by Chandragupta Maurya around 321 BCE. His grandson, Emperor Ashoka, ruled in the 3rd century BCE. During this period, the construction of large stone monuments became an important expression of royal authority, religious patronage and artistic skill.

Ashoka used inscriptions to communicate his ideas of dhamma, or ethical conduct, to people across his empire. These messages encouraged respect for elders, kindness towards living beings, proper treatment of servants and tolerance towards different religious traditions. The inscriptions were engraved on natural rock surfaces as well as on specially erected stone pillars.

Most Ashokan inscriptions were composed in Prakrit and written in the Brahmi script. In the northwestern regions, some inscriptions used Kharoshthi, Greek or Aramaic. Consequently, identifying an inscription as Ashokan does not mean that it must be written in Brahmi or that it must be carved on a pillar.

Construction and appearance of Ashokan pillars

An Ashokan pillar is generally recognised by its tall, carefully shaped stone shaft and its sculptured capital. The shaft was usually carved from a single block of sandstone, making it monolithic. Its surface was often finished with a high polish that gave the stone a smooth, almost shining appearance.

The shaft is the long vertical part of the pillar. The capital is the ornamental upper portion. Although the shaft was generally monolithic, the complete pillar could include a separately carved capital placed above it. Therefore, describing an Ashokan shaft as monolithic does not require every component of the monument to have been carved from one continuous stone.

The capitals frequently featured powerful animal figures, especially lions, bulls and elephants. These animals were placed above a decorated supporting member known as an abacus. The capital could also incorporate an inverted lotus or bell-shaped element.

Monolithic pillar

A monolithic pillar shaft is carved from one large stone rather than assembled from several separate stone drums.

Relationship with Achaemenid Persian architecture

Before the Mauryas, the Achaemenid rulers of Persia had developed a tradition of impressive stone columns, particularly in their royal buildings. The use of stone columns, animal forms and bell-shaped elements provides a basis for recognising a connection between Achaemenid and Mauryan architectural traditions.

However, the Ashokan pillar was not simply an Achaemenid column reproduced in India. Mauryan artisans developed a distinctive form, especially through the polished monolithic shaft and the arrangement of independent animal capitals.

FeatureMauryan pillarsAchaemenid columns
Main settingFrequently erected as independent monumentsCommonly formed part of large palace buildings
Shaft constructionUsually carved from a single stoneUsually assembled from separate stone sections
Shaft surfaceGenerally plain and highly polishedFrequently fluted, with vertical grooves
CapitalIndependent animal figures above an abacusAnimal and ornamental forms associated with architectural columns

The most useful distinction is structural: Mauryan pillars generally have plain, polished, monolithic shafts, whereas Achaemenid columns were commonly built from separate sections. Similarities in individual motifs should not obscure this difference.

Important Ashokan pillar sites

Several surviving capitals and pillars allow the features of Mauryan workmanship to be identified through actual examples.

  • Sarnath, Uttar Pradesh: The celebrated capital has 4 lions seated back to back. It later became the source of India's State Emblem.
  • Rampurva, Bihar: A finely polished bull capital is an important example of Mauryan animal sculpture.
  • Lauriya-Nandangarh, Bihar: An Ashokan pillar associated with a lion capital demonstrates the wider distribution of pillar monuments.
  • Sankisa, Uttar Pradesh: The site is associated with an elephant capital.
  • Vaishali region, Bihar: A lion-capital pillar survives at the site commonly identified as Basarh or Bakhira.

Not every Ashokan monument is a pillar. At Girnar near Junagadh in Gujarat, Ashoka's messages were engraved on a natural rock surface. This provides an important regional example of Mauryan inscriptions, but it must not be identified as an Ashokan pillar capital.

Prelims focus

  • Ashokan pillars belong to the Mauryan period, especially the 3rd century BCE.
  • Mauryan pillar shafts are generally monolithic, plain and polished.
  • Achaemenid columns were commonly constructed from separate sections.
  • Sarnath is associated with a lion capital; Rampurva is associated with a bull capital.
  • Most Ashokan inscriptions use Prakrit and Brahmi, with regional exceptions.
  • Trap: The Ashokan inscriptions at Girnar are rock edicts, not evidence of a standing Ashokan pillar at that site.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 3, Arts of the Mauryan Period, printed pp. 19–20; NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 8, Ashoka, the Emperor Who Gave Up War, printed pp. 75 and 79–80, 2018–19 reprint; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 2, Kings, Farmers and Towns, printed pp. 32–33; Government of Gujarat, Junagadh District, Ashok Shilalekh, consulted 23 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Stone carving and polishing were important achievements of Mauryan craftsmanship.

body:
Why the Sarnath capital is important

The Lion Capital of Ashoka at Sarnath, near Varanasi in Uttar Pradesh, is one of the finest surviving examples of Mauryan stone sculpture. It was erected during Ashoka's reign in the 3rd century BCE.

Sarnath is the place traditionally associated with the Buddha's first sermon after attaining enlightenment. This event is known as Dharmachakrapravartana, meaning the setting in motion of the Wheel of Dharma. The capital's association with the wheel therefore has a specific Buddhist significance.

The original Lion Capital is preserved in the archaeological museum at Sarnath. Its importance extends beyond ancient art because an adaptation of it was adopted as the State Emblem of India on 26 January 1950.

Parts of the original Lion Capital

The original monument consisted of a stone pillar shaft and an elaborate sculptured upper portion. The most important elements can be understood from the bottom upwards.

  • Pillar shaft: The tall stone column supporting the capital. The surviving shaft is broken.
  • Inverted lotus: A bell-shaped lotus form supporting the upper portion of the capital.
  • Circular abacus: A decorated band carrying animal figures and wheels.
  • 4 lions: Four powerful lions placed back to back, facing outward in different directions.
  • Crowning wheel: A large Dharma wheel that originally surmounted the lions. It has not survived intact.

The circular abacus depicts an elephant, a horse, a bull and a lion, separated by Dharma wheels. The wheels are represented with 24 spokes. The animals appear in movement, demonstrating the sculptors' ability to convey strength and vitality in stone.

The lions have carefully modelled bodies and manes. The polished sandstone surface is characteristic of the high standard of Mauryan workmanship. The capital was designed to be viewed from different directions, rather than as a sculpture intended for only one frontal view.

4 lions, not 3

The original Sarnath capital contains 4 lions. In a frontal representation, only 3 lions are visible because the fourth faces away from the viewer.

How the State Emblem differs from the original

India's State Emblem is an adaptation of the Sarnath capital, not a reproduction of every component of the original monument. Its official description is set out in the Schedule to the State Emblem of India (Prohibition of Improper Use) Act, 2005.

The official emblem shows the profile of 3 visible lions above the abacus. On the visible portion of the abacus, the Dharma Chakra appears in the centre, a bull on the right and a galloping horse on the left. Outlines of wheels appear towards the outer sides.

The bell-shaped lotus beneath the original capital is omitted. The large wheel that originally crowned the lions is also not part of the adopted emblem's design. The motto Satyameva Jayate, meaning Truth Alone Triumphs, appears beneath the emblem. The motto comes from the Mundaka Upanishad; it is not an inscription that Ashoka originally placed beneath the lions.

Distinguishing the historical object from the modern emblem

Questions may refer either to the archaeological sculpture or to the officially adopted State Emblem. The answer depends on which object is being described. A statement about 4 lions is correct for the original sculpture, while a statement about 3 visible lions describes the adopted frontal profile. Similarly, the original has a bell-shaped lotus, but the official emblem omits it.

The date also matters. The original capital belongs to the Mauryan period in the 3rd century BCE; the modern State Emblem was adopted in 1950. The 2005 Act describes and regulates the emblem's use; it did not create the original Mauryan sculpture.

Prelims focus

  • The Sarnath Lion Capital was made under Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE.
  • The original capital has 4 lions, a circular abacus and an inverted lotus.
  • The abacus depicts an elephant, horse, bull and lion, separated by Dharma wheels.
  • The State Emblem was adopted on 26 January 1950.
  • The official emblem omits the lotus and includes the motto Satyameva Jayate.
  • Trap: The modern State Emblem shows 3 visible lions, but the original sculpture contains 4.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 3, Arts of the Mauryan Period, printed pp. 20 and 22–23; Government of India, State Emblem of India (Prohibition of Improper Use) Act, 2005, Schedule, Description and Design, consulted 23 November 2026; Government of India, National Portal of India, National Identity, State Emblem, consulted 23 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: The original Sarnath Lion Capital is a Mauryan sculpture with 4 lions above a decorated circular abacus.

body:
What is a stupa?

The word stupa originally refers to a mound or heap. In Buddhist architecture, a stupa became a sacred monument associated with the Buddha, his teachings, important events or the remains of revered religious figures.

Many early stupas were constructed over relics, such as bodily remains of the Buddha or objects associated with him. These remains might be placed inside a relic casket within the mound. Such monuments became places of reverence because they symbolised the presence and memory of the Buddha.

The tradition of making burial mounds existed before Buddhism, but stupas acquired particular religious importance within Buddhist practice. Not every surviving stupa necessarily contains the Buddha's bodily relics. Some contain the remains of other revered persons, while others were built as commemorative or devotional monuments.

Major structural parts of a stupa

The earliest stupas were relatively simple mounds. Over time, additional architectural features made them more elaborate. The following terms identify the principal parts of the developed stupa form.

  • Anda: The large hemispherical or dome-like mound forming the main body of the stupa.
  • Relic casket: A container placed within the monument to preserve sacred remains or associated objects, where such relics were deposited.
  • Medhi or drum: The raised supporting portion beneath the dome. In developed stupas, a terrace could also provide an upper circumambulatory path.
  • Harmika: A small square enclosure constructed at the top of the anda.
  • Yashti: The vertical mast rising from the harmika.
  • Chhatra: An umbrella-like element mounted on the yashti, symbolising honour and spiritual significance.
  • Vedika: The railing marking the sacred area and defining the movement of devotees.
  • Torana: An ornamental entrance gateway. Elaborately decorated toranas were added to several important stupas.
  • Pradakshinapatha: The path used by devotees to walk around the sacred monument.

Why devotees walk clockwise around a stupa

Pradakshina means circumambulation, or moving around a sacred object as an act of reverence. At a Buddhist stupa, worshippers generally move clockwise, keeping the monument on their right.

The railing and gateways organise this movement. At larger stupas, the lower circumambulatory path may be supplemented by an upper path reached by steps. The physical arrangement therefore reflects the religious practice associated with the monument.

Pradakshinapatha

A pradakshinapatha is the designated route around a sacred structure used for ritual circumambulation. At Buddhist stupas, the customary direction is clockwise.

Stupa, chaitya and vihara are different structures

These 3 terms often occur together because Buddhist religious establishments could contain all of them. Their functions, however, are different.

TermMeaningMain function
StupaSacred mound or monumentVeneration of relics, memory or a sacred event
ChaityaSacred shrine or worship hallCongregational worship; a chaitya hall may contain a stupa
ViharaMonastic residenceAccommodation and daily activities of monks or nuns

A stupa does not become a vihara because monks live nearby. Equally, a chaitya hall and the stupa contained inside it are not identical architectural elements.

How stupas were supported and decorated

Royal patronage was important, especially under Ashoka, but stupa construction was not financed exclusively by kings. Inscriptions record donations by merchants, craft guilds, monks, nuns and ordinary devotees. At Sanchi, members of an ivory-workers' guild contributed towards a gateway.

Later railings and gateways provided surfaces for sculptors to depict the life of the Buddha and the Jataka stories, which relate accounts of the Buddha's previous births. The carvings helped communicate religious narratives through recognisable scenes.

In early Buddhist art, the Buddha was frequently represented symbolically rather than in human form. An empty seat, a Bodhi tree, footprints, a stupa or a Dharma wheel could refer to his presence or particular events in his life. The Dharma wheel, for example, is strongly associated with the first sermon at Sarnath.

Human images of the Buddha subsequently became widespread, particularly through the sculptural traditions associated with Mathura and other centres. Thus, an early stupa relief using an empty throne and a later sculpture showing the seated Buddha can refer to the same religious figure through different artistic conventions.

Prelims focus

  • Anda is the main dome-like mound of a stupa.
  • Harmika is the small square enclosure above the dome.
  • Yashti is the mast and chhatra is the umbrella-like crowning element.
  • Vedika means railing; torana means gateway.
  • Pradakshina is performed clockwise, keeping the stupa on the right.
  • Trap: A stupa is a sacred monument, a chaitya is a shrine or worship hall, and a vihara is a monastic residence.

[Sources: NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 4, Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings, printed pp. 96–97 and 100–101; NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 12, Buildings, Paintings and Books, printed pp. 122–125, 2018–19 reprint; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 3, Arts of the Mauryan Period, printed pp. 21 and 26.]
